latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable bacteria enter orbital fat, extraocular muscle sheaths, periosteum, or lacrimal/orbital soft tissue posterior to the orbital septum. This distinguishes orbital cellulitis from isolated preseptal cellulitis.

Ethmoid, maxillary, frontal, or sphenoid sinus infection spreads through thin lamina papyracea, valveless venous channels, or bony dehiscence into the orbit. This is the common pathway in children and many community cases.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Dental, skin, trauma, lacrimal, or postoperative inoculation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Odontogenic infection, facial cellulitis, eyelid trauma, penetrating foreign material, dacryocystitis, orbital surgery, or hematogenous seeding directly introduces polymicrobial bacteria into orbital or periorbital tissues.

Innate immune activation in the confined orbit causes vascular leak, inflammatory edema, purulence, orbital fat stranding, extraocular muscle edema, chemosis, pain, fever, leukocytosis, CRP, and ESR elevation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Orbital compartment pressure and optic nerve stress
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflammatory edema, proptosis, abscess mass effect, orbital apex crowding, and vascular compromise restrict eye movement and threaten optic nerve perfusion, producing diplopia, reduced acuity, afferent pupillary defect, and permanent vision loss.

Localized pus collects beneath periosteum or within orbital soft tissue when bacterial burden and anatomic obstruction exceed host clearance. Abscess often requires drainage or source control in addition to antibiotics.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Venous, cavernous sinus, and intracranial spread
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Infection extends through valveless ophthalmic venous drainage, orbital apex, skull base, or contiguous bone to cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, epidural/subdural infection, brain abscess, cranial neuropathies, or septic emboli.

High bacterial burden, invasive gram-negative or staphylococcal infection, delayed control, or intracranial spread can produce positive blood cultures, systemic inflammatory response, hypotension, organ dysfunction, and mortality risk.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sinus infection is the most common contiguous source crossing thin orbital walls or venous channels.

Orbital bacterial invasion triggers rapid innate inflammation and edema.

Persistent bacterial growth and poor drainage create subperiosteal or orbital pus collections.
Abscess mass effect worsens proptosis, pressure, motility restriction, and optic nerve compromise.
Orbital infection can extend through ophthalmic veins, orbital apex, bone, or skull-base routes to cavernous sinus or CNS.
Invasive bacterial orbital infection can seed blood or produce systemic inflammatory and septic physiology.
Sinusitis is the parent source finding for many orbital cellulitis cases.
Toothache, dental caries, gum abscess, periapical lucency, or maxillary sinus floor erosion identify odontogenic source.
Penetrating injury, chemical/particulate contamination, facial cellulitis, or postoperative wounds can directly seed orbital tissues.
Edema of eyelids and periorbital soft tissue is common but not specific.
Inflamed eyelids are typical and overlap with preseptal cellulitis.

Pain worsens with extraocular muscle traction in postseptal orbital inflammation.
Orbital edema and abscess push the globe forward.
Venous congestion and conjunctival inflammation produce chemosis.
Edematous or entrapped extraocular muscles restrict eye movement.
Motility restriction causes binocular diplopia.
Lid edema, levator inflammation, or cranial nerve involvement can cause ptosis.
Optic nerve compression, keratopathy, abscess mass effect, or vascular compromise reduce acuity.
Afferent defect is a warning sign for optic nerve compromise.
CT/MRI postseptal fat inflammation is the imaging anchor.
Orbital fat stranding measures inflammatory spread.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Sinusitis is a common source and increases likelihood of postseptal spread.
Odontogenic orbital cellulitis often forms abscess and needs procedural source control.
Postseptal edema and mass effect produce proptosis.
Greater orbital mass effect tends to restrict motility.
Diplopia tracks motility restriction but may be unreportable in young children or severe swelling.
Orbital abscess usually increases the need for drainage or debridement.
Subperiosteal abscess may need surgical or endoscopic drainage depending on size, age, vision, and response.
Active antibiotics lower inflammatory markers after a lag.
Worse acuity at presentation indicates optic nerve or ocular compromise and higher permanent vision loss risk.
RAPD is a high-risk optic nerve sign.
Cavernous sinus and skull-base spread increases CNS infection risk.
Meningitis is a major life-threatening complication.
Brain abscess or empyema raises mortality hazard and source-control need.
Septic physiology is the systemic mortality pathway.

Ampicillin-sulbactam does not reliably cover MRSA.
ESBL gram-negative orbital infection may require carbapenem-active therapy.
Covers many oral streptococci and anaerobes when susceptible.

supportive_care: Urgent ophthalmology assessment with visual acuity, pupils/RAPD, intraocular pressure, color vision when feasible, ocular motility, proptosis, and fundus/optic nerve evaluation.
Contrast CT or MRI of orbits and sinuses when postseptal signs are present, vision is affected, motility is restricted, abscess is suspected, neurologic signs exist, or response is poor.
ENT, ophthalmology, dentistry/oral surgery, infectious diseases, and neurosurgery coordination according to sinus, dental, orbital abscess, or intracranial involvement.
Serial eye examinations because abscess, optic nerve compromise, or intracranial spread can emerge after apparently improving eyelid swelling.
Culture blood, drainage material, sinus/dental/foreign-body source, or conjunctival/orbital pus when obtainable, but do not delay empiric antimicrobial treatment for cultures.
Monitor fever curve, pain, swelling, motility, visual acuity, WBC/CRP, renal function, antimicrobial toxicity, and need for renal dosing.
Protect ocular surface with lubrication, moisture chamber, eyelid care, and exposure keratopathy prevention when proptosis or incomplete closure is present.

Assess for cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, septic emboli, or stroke when headache, cranial neuropathy, altered mental status, focal deficit, meningeal signs, or persistent bacteremia appears.
Avoid labeling isolated eyelid swelling as orbital cellulitis without postseptal clues; preseptal cellulitis remains a near mimic and should rank on its own manifold when available.
After acute control, ensure dental, sinus, lacrimal, trauma, or immune-risk follow-up to prevent relapse.
